meta.title: More Likely Than Not, Three Times Over
meta.theme: why deciding each element of a claim on the balance of probabilities can decide the claim itself against the probabilities

format.format_verified: 2026-09: five sentences, TITA, +3 with no negative marking, consistent in released papers 2016 to 2025; re-verify against each new official paper

traps.description: The outlier is the sentence a textbook would put first, a general account of what a standard of proof is for, and it shares the paragraph's central phrase. The decoy is the closing sentence, which leaves the arithmetic for what courts actually ask and so looks like a change of subject from theory to practice.

meta.learning_objective: build the specific chain first, so that a general statement about the same subject can be tested for whether any link of the chain uses it

quality.adversarial_review: The rival is the closing sentence about what courts actually ask: it moves from arithmetic to practice and can look like the start of a separate discussion of how judges behave. It stays because it answers the objection the sentence before it raises, and because changing what is weighed is a reply to the multiplication and to nothing else in the set. The general statement about allocating the risk of error is the sentence a chapter would open with; here no step turns on why the standard sits where it does, only on what happens when a standard is applied three times over.

source.usage_note: Original composition in CAT register for CAT OS. General account of the conjunction problem in civil proof; no specific text adapted. Personal study only.

meta.reviewer_notes: A ninety-nine item whose outlier is the most quotable sentence in the set and would open a chapter on the same subject. The core is a tight specific chain, so the uniqueness test is decisive once the learner builds before eliminating.

sentences.label: A
sentences.text: Three findings each a little past a half can multiply to something well below a half, so a defendant may be held liable on a story that is more likely false than true.

sentences.label: B
sentences.text: A civil claim ordinarily comes in parts: that the defendant owed a duty, that he fell short of it, and that the shortfall caused the loss complained of.

sentences.label: C
sentences.text: A standard of proof allocates the risk of error between the parties, and its height records how much worse one kind of mistake is thought to be than the other.

sentences.label: D
sentences.text: Each part is decided on the balance of probabilities, so a claimant who carries every one of them at fifty-one per cent has carried the claim.

sentences.label: E
sentences.text: Courts keep clear of the multiplication by asking instead whether the claimant's account taken whole is likelier than the defendant's, which meets the objection by changing what is being weighed.

builder.prompt: Build the four-sentence explanation of how a claim proved part by part can still be improbable as a whole. The sentence that states a general truth no step of that explanation uses is your answer.

explanation.spine_note: The core explains one difficulty in four steps. It opens with the fact that a civil claim has separable parts, then states how each is decided and what follows when a claimant carries them all at bare majority. The third step performs the multiplication and names the uncomfortable result, and the fourth gives the way courts avoid it and what that avoidance costs. Structure, rule, consequence, response.

core_roles.label: B
core_roles.why_here: The whole problem depends on a claim having parts, and this is the only sentence that says so or names them.

core_roles.label: D
core_roles.why_here: It applies the standard to the parts just listed, and its fifty-one per cent supplies the number the next sentence multiplies.

core_roles.label: A
core_roles.why_here: It draws the arithmetic consequence of the rule just stated, which is the difficulty the paragraph exists to display.

core_roles.label: E
core_roles.why_here: It answers the difficulty directly, and can only come last because there is nothing for a court to keep clear of until the multiplication has been performed.

links.explanation: 'Each part' points at the three elements just listed and applies a single rule to all of them.
The bare majority on each element is now given, and the new material is what those majorities do when they are combined.
'The multiplication' names the operation the previous sentence performed, so the response is tied to the difficulty rather than merely following it.

explanation.violation_named: The odd sentence states in general terms what a standard of proof is for. The four core sentences work through one specific consequence of applying a particular standard to a claim with parts, and not one of their steps turns on why the standard sits at the height it does or on how the risk of error is shared.
explanation.why_it_breaks: The chain runs from parts to a rule to a product to a judicial response, and each link takes its material from the one before. A statement about allocating risk receives nothing from the elements of a claim and hands nothing to the multiplication, so wherever it is placed the chain stops for a line. It is also answering a different question, why the standard is set where it is, when the paragraph is asking what happens when it is applied more than once.
explanation.trap_exposed: The disguise is authority. It is the sentence a textbook chapter would open with, it uses the paragraph's own central phrase, and a reader who feels the set lacks a definition will fit it at the front. The decoy is the closing sentence, which leaves arithmetic for practice and so appears to change the subject, though it is the only sentence that answers the difficulty the paragraph has taken the trouble to build.

exclusion_analysis.label: B
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It is a plain statement of legal structure with no argument in it, so a reader looking for the paragraph's point may treat it as preliminary matter.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it there are no parts, so each part has nothing to refer to and the multiplication has nothing to multiply.

exclusion_analysis.label: D
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It looks like a restatement of the standard rather than a step, and its number can seem decorative until the next sentence uses it.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the paragraph never says how the parts are decided, and the arithmetic operates on findings the reader has no reason to think are near a half.

exclusion_analysis.label: A
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It is the only sentence that does arithmetic, and its register sounds more like probability than law.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the difficulty is never stated, and the closing sentence keeps courts clear of a multiplication the paragraph never performed.

exclusion_analysis.label: E
exclusion_analysis.why_tempting: It describes what courts do rather than what follows logically, so it can look like the opening of a separate discussion of judicial practice.
exclusion_analysis.what_breaks: Without it the exposition raises an objection and abandons it, and the reader is left with a paradox rather than an account of how the law lives with one.

explanation.detection_habit: Build the specific chain link by link before you judge any sentence. Once the chain exists, a general truth about the same subject either carries a link or it is standing beside the chain looking authoritative.

mentor.challenge: Five sentences about proof in a civil court, and one of them is the sentence you would expect to find first. Build the chain before deciding where it belongs.
mentor.takeaway: Definitions are not free. A general statement belongs only where a later sentence stands on it.
